summary: Celecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor NSAID used for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile RA, ankylosing spondylitis, acute pain and primary dysmenorrhea. It offers lower gastrointestinal ulcer risk than non-selective NSAIDs but carries the NSAID-class boxed warning for serious cardiovascular thrombotic events and gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration and perforation. It is contraindicated in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft surgery and in patients with sulfonamide or aspirin/NSAID hypersensitivity. Dose is reduced by half in moderate hepatic impairment and in CYP2C9 poor metabolizers. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration.

moa: Selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), reducing synthesis of inflammatory prostaglandins (notably prostaglandin E2) while largely sparing COX-1-mediated gastric mucosal and platelet prostaglandins, producing anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to celecoxib (anaphylaxis, serious skin reactions)
Aspirin- or NSAID-induced asthma, urticaria or allergic reactions
In the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
relative: Established cardiovascular disease or significant CV risk factors

preg: Avoid; NSAIDs may cause fetal renal dysfunction and oligohydramnios from about 20 weeks, and premature closure of the ductus arteriosus from 30 weeks (third trimester), where use is contraindicated. May also impair fertility/ovulation and delay parturition.
lact: Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; generally considered compatible with breastfeeding, but use the lowest effective dose and monitor the infant.
renal: Not recommended in advanced renal disease; if used, monitor renal function closely. Risk of fluid retention, edema and acute kidney injury, especially with volume depletion, heart failure, or concomitant ACE inhibitors/ARBs/diuretics.
hepatic: Reduce the daily dose by 50% in moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B). Not recommended in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). Discontinue if liver enzymes worsen or signs of liver disease develop.

major: Aspirin / other NSAIDs - increased GI toxicity (and loss of COX-2 GI benefit)
Drugs metabolized by CYP2D6 - celecoxib inhibits CYP2D6

CYP2C9 inhibitors (e.g. fluconazole) - increased celecoxib levels
minor: Antacids (aluminum/magnesium) - slight reduction in celecoxib absorption

missed: Take when remembered unless it is near the next scheduled dose, then skip the missed dose; do not double up.
overdose: May cause lethargy, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain, with GI bleeding, hypertension, acute renal failure, respiratory depression and coma in severe cases. Management is supportive with airway/cardiovascular monitoring; activated charcoal may help if given within 1-2 hours. There is no specific antidote and hemodialysis is unlikely to be useful due to high protein binding.
